Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-118740 affectant Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-x64 (nuget) (score CVSS 9.1).

Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-118740 - Aspire Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability

Aspire Dashboard's unauthenticated NotFound route can permit telemetry deletion in both standalone and AppHost-hosted deployments. In standalone deployments using browser-token authentication, it can also expose the browser token.

Announcement for this issue can be found at dotnet/announcements#526

Both 13.6.3 and 13.6.4 contain the unauthenticated NotFound route.

Aspire Dashboard releases through 13.6.4 are affected, whether deployed independently or launched by an Aspire AppHost. For an AppHost using Dashboard SDK packages, check the resolved Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk package versions against the affected ranges above. If the AppHost selects a CLI-bundled Dashboard or a custom Dashboard path, check the version of that Dashboard instead. Aspire ships independently of .NET; installing a .NET runtime or SDK update does not replace the Dashboard.

Update Aspire Dashboard to version 13.6.5 or later. Neither 13.6.3 nor 13.6.4 is a fixed upgrade target.

For container deployments, explicitly set the Dashboard image to mcr.microsoft.com/aspire/dashboard:13.6.5 and recreate or redeploy the container. Replace older version tags and nightly image references, including those in generated Docker Compose or Kubernetes manifests, with this fixed stable image. Updating AppHost package references alone does not replace an image reference in an existing deployment manifest.

items.body:

Public SignDrop exploit code abuses Windows CLFS log authentication to enable local SYSTEM privilege escalation, with no Microsoft fix available.

The proof of concept, called SignDrop , targets a log-authentication feature added to the driver last year.
items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique affectant Windows.

Public SignDrop exploit code abuses Windows CLFS log authentication to enable local SYSTEM privilege escalation, with no Microsoft fix available.

Public exploit code released earlier this week claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System driver.

The proof of concept, called SignDrop , targets a log-authentication feature added to the driver last year. It abuses how clfs.sys creates companion files when a privileged process opens a prepared log, using path redirection to take control of the operation. Microsoft has not confirmed the claimed flaw, assigned a CVE, or released a fix.

The researcher behind the exploit, who publishes under the name MSNightmare , released the code and a detailed writeup on GitHub on Tuesday, the same day the company published its November security updates.

CLFS is a logging subsystem built into Windows. Its driver has been a frequent target for privilege escalation: 10 CLFS flaws appear in CISA's catalog of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in attacks, including one used in ransomware campaigns in April 2025.

To reduce that exposure, Microsoft added an authentication check to CLFS log files in updates for Windows 11 25H2, 26H1, and Windows Server 2025 shipped in October 2025. The check attaches a hash-based message authentication code, built from log data and a key unique to each machine.

The driver then parses only log files it wrote. A companion .cnpf file stores recovery data beside each log and is created with the same security attributes as the original, according to the company's logfile authentication page.

items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-100397 affectant rucio (pip) (score CVSS 9.8).

Rucio: Unauthenticated administrator impersonation through SSH challenge tokens

While an SSH challenge token is intended as a short-lived nonce for use in a subsequent SSH key exchange, the function to validate authentication tokens does not differentiate between these and actual authentication tokens. Because challenge tokens are generated based on an account name provided via headers without requiring prior authentication, an unauthenticated attacker can request a valid "challenge" token for any account (including administrative ones) and use it to authenticate against other API endpoints.

The vulnerability exists because SSH challenge tokens are stored in the same database table as regular authentication tokens and validate_auth_token in lib/rucio/core/authentication.py accepts these "challenge" tokens. An attacker can obtain a challenge token for an account such as “root” via the REST API and then present it as a valid authentication bearer token:

items.body:

Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file write and read in image analysis

ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one.

The Department of Justice and FBI announced two separate actions in response to North Korea-linked cryptocurrency theft operations.

Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said multiple divisions within the Justice Department “played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach.”

“As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach,” Duva said.

Binance and the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor — the premiere North Korean hacking group responsible for stealing billions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency in multiple attacks over the last decade.

“Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges,” the Justice Department said.

Multiple blockchain security firms said North Korea and other actors are using novel, automated methods to launder the stolen cryptocurrency.

Michael Barnhart, a nation-state threat researcher at DTEX who has spent years tracking North Korean cybercrime campaigns, previously told Recorded Future News that TraderTraitor's modus operandi is to immediately offload stolen funds to Chinese money launderers for a lump sum or percentage.

Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

The incident is the latest in a string of attacks on ports and other shipping organizations worldwide, with Brazil’s largest port hit with ransomware last week.

Danish shipping company Maersk said threat actors gained access to a “legacy system from a previous acquisition,” but said the incident does not impact other parts of the firm.

Maersk said its findings suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it does not anticipate disruptions for customers. “The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI,” the company said.

Maersk provided few details on the attack but the statement came three days after the WhiteArmor ransomware gang claimed it attacked LF Logistics. The Hong-Kong based transportation and logistics company was acquired by Maersk in 2022.

Maersk, which has previously dealt with ransomware affecting company systems as well as specific port operations , is not the only shipping organization to be dealing with a cyber incident.

An attack on Brazil’s Santos Port Authority — one of the largest in South America — began last Friday and caused a power outage, eventually leading to significant delays in loading and unloading cargo while also forcing officials to conduct route scheduling and billing services manually.

The Santos Port Authority said on Thursday that it has been able to recover about 70% of its systems through backups. Brazil’s Federal Police are now investigating the attack.

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par Security Affairs.

Europe’s spyware victims face years of legal battles and few answers as governments shield surveillance behind national security. Greek journalist Thanasis Koukakis waited almost five years for a court to confirm what happened to him. His phone was infected with the infaous spyware Predator that gave whoever was watching access to his contacts, documents and messages, and even let them switch on his camera and microphone. IrpiMedia’s journalist and researcher Rosita Rijtano interviewed him and four other victims in a long investigation, and the picture it paints is bleak. On February 26, a court in Athens convicted four executives linked to Intellexa , the company behind the Predator spyware. They include its founder, Tal Dilian , a former Israeli military intelligence commander. They face prison sentences of up to eight years for illegally accessing computer systems, violating data protection rules and breaking telecommunications privacy laws. Their sentences are suspended while they appeal, and investigators have not identified who ordered the surveillance. This is the first conviction of its kind in Europe, highlighting how rare such cases are. The scandal began in 2021, when an international investigation led by Forbidden Stories revealed that dozens of European activists, politicians and journalists had been targeted with Pegasus spyware, developed by NSO Group

Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

Abuse of an independent third-party tool led to breaches at ScreenConnect customers, confirmed the software's maker, ConnectWise. Cybersecurity researchers had spotted intrusions at nearly 50.

IT management software company ConnectWise said it is investigating reports of unauthorized access to its customers following reports from multiple cybersecurity firms that almost 50 organizations had been breached through the company’s ScreenConnect tool.

Late on Wednesday evening, ConnectWise said it believes the activity is related to the abuse of an independent third-party extension installed in customer environments. The tool, RMM+, is an extension for ConnectWise ScreenConnect that allows external management tools to automate and control remote sessions through an API.

“We identified approximately 400 partner environments with at least one independently developed third-party extension from the RMM+ family installed. Their presence alone does not establish compromise,” the company said.

“These extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands. Access to that API is protected by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup.”

The Tampa-based company told customers that threat actors were deploying additional remote-access software and also saw “potential compromise of technician workstations during interactive connections to affected devices. “

The company disabled RMM+ in the 400 customer environments and urged customers with on-premises systems to disable it themselves because ConnectWise cannot do it for them. All customers should verify that RMM+ is disabled.

“Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases" and more, United Airlines said.

United Airlines will block AI agents from managing customers’ reservations and flight purchases, warning of significant cybersecurity and privacy risks, as well as potential legal violations.

Other large corporations have made similar announcements recently, including Bank of America, which cautioned users last week to never share user IDs and passwords with agents.

Many companies, particularly banks and airlines, have faced mounting difficulty as they try to separate human customers from their AI assistants. The firms warn that consumers’ credentials are at risk of leaking when they entrust agents with their logins and passwords.

“Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” United said in a Wednesday press release .

Automated AI actions also could break Federal Aviation Administration and Department of Transportation rules, the release said, citing the fact that flight check-in requires “human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.”

The airline is implementing the new access restrictions both within its own digital platforms and separately through aggregators and agencies.

It would be a “betrayal of the democratic process” if Congress included a straightforward renewal of a controversial lapsed surveillance law in the annual defense policy bill, a collection of civil liberties groups wrote to Hill leaders Thursday. Lawmakers weren’t able to agree this summer to a long-term extension of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, under which the government can use Americans’ personal information without a warrant to search for their communications with foreign targets. A court has authorized such searches through March despite the law’s lapse. Congress in 2023 authorized a short-term extension of Section 702 through the annual, “must-pass” National Defense Authorization Act in a move protested by civil liberties groups and some lawmakers at the time. Signal de veille — Infosecurity Mag.

Fortinet finds weak SQL Server passwords used to deliver a miner and Gh0st RAT

A campaign has been breaking into internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances with weak passwords to install a Monero cryptominer and a Gh0st remote access trojan (RAT).

FortiGuard Labs, Fortinet's research team, uncovered the campaign in early October 2026 and rated it high severity, according to new research published on November 12. The report did not say how many servers were compromised or who was behind the campaign.

The initial Go payload contained the open-source Naabu port scanner. It retrieved an IP range from its server, scanned it for TCP port 1433, the default SQL Server port, and recorded the hosts that responded, before requesting another range and starting again.

A brute-force tool then tried usernames including "sa" and "admin" against more than 2700 passwords on each host the scanner found.

After a successful login, the malware ran Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands on the server. T-SQL is SQL Server's extension of the SQL database language, adding programming features to standard queries.

The commands enabled xp_cmdshell, which runs operating system commands, then downloaded or unpacked a loader. They also scheduled the loader to run daily and placed a copy in the Startup folder so it ran when the server booted.
